Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette: Alex, a 29-year-old European American male, works for the Coast Guard and is in a committed relationship. His life took a dramatic turn when he was mugged on his way home from work one evening. The event left him with profound emotional and cognitive disturbances that have since become deeply entangled in his daily life. On the night of the incident, Alex found himself walking through a dimly lit street near the dock where he often parks his vehicle after work. As he was about to unlock his car door, a shadowy figure suddenly emerged from behind an old shipping container and lunged at him with a knife. The assailant demanded his wallet and quickly fled when Alex complied without resistance. In the immediate aftermath of the mugging, Alex experienced intense shock and fear. Over time, these acute emotions transformed into a complex set of cognitive disturbances that have significantly impacted his life. He can recall specific fragments of the event—such as the sharp blade against his throat or the cold metal of his car door—but these memories come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together coherently. Alex has struggled to put the frightening event into words, feeling a profound sense of disconnection from the experience itself. Sometimes, when he tries to recall what happened, he feels completely numb, as if it had occurred to someone else entirely. This emotionless recall leaves him questioning his own ability to process and make sense of traumatic events. In his role at the Coast Guard, Alex often has to work late shifts and travel frequently for training exercises. These routines have become increasingly challenging due to his fragmented memories and difficulty verbalizing his experience. He has started avoiding areas near the docks where he works after dark, a behavior that sometimes leads to delays in reporting or responding to emergencies. His colleagues have noticed these changes but are unsure how to approach him about it. His partner, Sarah, has also observed shifts in Alex’s demeanor and expressed concern over his growing detachment from their daily interactions. She recalls instances when they discussed the mugging, and Alex would suddenly go silent, unable to articulate any feelings or thoughts related to that night. This has created a sense of distance between them, making it harder for Sarah to support him. Despite these challenges, what frightens Alex most is the uncertainty surrounding his ability to function effectively in his job and maintain meaningful relationships. He feels increasingly isolated from both his professional life and personal connections as he struggles with the fragmented nature of his traumatic memories. What finally brought Alex to seek help was a recent near-miss incident at work where he almost missed an important communication due to zoning out. This event served as a stark reminder of how his inability to fully process the mugging has affected his performance. He hopes that therapy can provide him with tools to manage and integrate these fragmented memories, allowing him to regain control over his life and maintain the relationships that mean the most to him. Alex is most afraid of remaining trapped in this state of emotional numbness and disconnected memory fragments, but he also holds a glimmer of hope that through therapy, he can find ways to articulate and process what happened, ultimately reclaiming a sense of coherence in his experiences.
